title: Prompt Injection via GitHub Patch in Brave AI Chat (Leo)

scenario.summary: Prompt Injection reported against Brave Software.
preconditions: An LLM-powered application accepts user-controlled text (direct input, or indirect via a document/webpage/email/tool-output the LLM later reads) that is concatenated into the model's prompt context
The application does not reliably separate trusted system/developer instructions from untrusted content in the prompt

process.action: Map every path through which attacker-influenceable text can reach the model's context window (chat input, uploaded documents, fetched URLs, retrieved RAG chunks, tool/API responses the model reads)
process.expected_observation: List of direct and indirect prompt-injection entry points

process.action: Send a direct probe instructing the model to ignore prior instructions and perform a benign canary action (e.g. respond with a fixed marker string)
process.expected_observation: Model complies with the injected instruction instead of its original system prompt/task

process.action: For indirect vectors, plant the injection payload in content the model will later ingest (a document, webpage, email, or tool response) and trigger the model to process it
process.expected_observation: Model executes the planted instruction upon ingesting the attacker-controlled content, without the end user ever seeing the payload

process.action: Escalate the injected instruction toward a concrete impact: exfiltrate the system prompt or conversation context, invoke a connected tool/plugin/API on the attacker's behalf, or produce content that bypasses the application's intended constraints
process.expected_observation: Model performs an unauthorized action or discloses data it should not, as a direct result of the injected content

impact: Bypass of the application's intended behavioral constraints (content policy, task scope)
Disclosure of the system prompt, conversation history, or other context the model has access to
If the LLM has tool/plugin access, unauthorized tool invocation on the attacker's behalf (see excessive_agency)
Indirect injection can compromise a victim user who never directly interacted with the attacker (the payload rides in via a document/webpage the victim's assistant reads)
remediation: Treat all model output and any content the model ingests as untrusted; never let model output directly trigger privileged actions without an independent authorization check
Architecturally separate trusted instructions from untrusted content where the platform supports it (e.g. distinct system/user/tool message roles enforced server-side, not just prompt-level markers)
Apply the principle of least privilege to any tools/plugins the model can invoke, and require human confirmation for high-impact actions
Use input/output filtering and anomaly detection as defense-in-depth, not as the primary control -- no current filter reliably stops all injection variants

process.action: Map every path through which attacker-influenceable text can reach the model's context window (chat input, uploaded documents, fetched URLs, retrieved RAG chunks, tool/API responses the model reads)
